name: Hana Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach voice before lunch, work on jingles or practice clips in the afternoon, and lead the Wednesday choir at night. My music master’s helps me hear tiny problems, but I earn less than people assume a conductor earns.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that work matters most to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When a shy singer finds a strong note beside someone else, I remember why I do it. Then I go home and count which pupils have actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir committee that AI can sort our rehearsal messages, which is fine by me. People still turn up to sing together and I still have to teach them to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am less calm about the rent than the technology. I conduct the choir and give voice lessons, but one quiet month leaves almost nothing in my account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep the Wednesday choir and my private pupils. This week I will use the AI scheduling assistant I already use to offer empty lesson slots, and put any extra fee into a rent jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hopeful about filling gaps and anxious about bills. A clever calendar cannot pay me until a pupil actually books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last empty lesson week cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two pupils dropped lessons during examination week, leaving me 80 short. If one new pupil takes those slots, the extra fees go straight to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide whether to trust that scheduling assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father repairs shoes and always says a tool earns its place by saving real work. I agree, but I check every message before it goes to a family.

say: I would tell the **choir committee** that AI can help schedule rehearsals.
I would say **breathing together** still takes people in the room.
think: My **thin savings** make an empty lesson week painful even without big AI change.
I trust tools only when they bring **paid pupils** into open slots.
do: Keep the **Wednesday choir** and private voice lessons this winter.
Offer open **lesson slots** through my current AI scheduling assistant this week.
feel: I feel **hopeful** about filling slots and anxious about rent.
S0.quote: A clever calendar cannot pay me until a pupil actually books.
fieldNote: Her daily **AI use** is practical and tied to paid lessons, not faith in technology.
The missed **80** last examination week explains her anxiety despite a senior choir role.

steps.text: Keep conducting the Wednesday choir and teaching voice pupils
Offer empty voice lesson slots through her AI scheduling assistant
Put any extra booked lesson fee into a rent jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that AI will take more booking, score checking and draft jingle work. I would ask the hall to pay us for the performance instead of treating a generated track as an excuse to lower the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My small advertising jingles could disappear, and the choir hall might spend less on a conductor if it can prepare rehearsal tracks itself. I can sell direct lessons, but I cannot assume every family keeps paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will test a four-week ear-training class at the church hall next month, if it lets me rent the room cheaply. During the first year I would use AI to make practice clips for paying pupils, check every note myself, and keep the fees separate from choir pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but busy. I would rather find out whether eight people pay for a class than complain about a lost jingle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many people make the new class worth running?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight people at 12 each would cover the hall and give me something for the evening. With four people, I would cancel the next block instead of borrowing to fill the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the hall manager for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the hall manager the cost of a live rehearsal, including the hours people do not see. I would ask for a written fee before the next term begins.

say: I would ask the hall for a **written live fee** even if rehearsal tracks become cheap.
I would explain the hidden **rehearsal hours** behind a performance.
think: My **jingle fees** may vanish as AI drafts music cheaply.
I need **eight paying pupils** before a new evening class can support me.
do: Test a **four-week ear class** next month with eight prepayments and low rent; cancel the next block if only four enroll.
Make and check **AI practice clips** for paying pupils during the first year.
Ask the hall manager for a **written live fee** before next term.
feel: I feel **anxious** about jingles, but testing a class gives me a choice.
S1.quote: I would rather find out whether eight people pay for a class than complain about a lost jingle.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive response** is a small paid trial with an enrollment threshold.
She uses **AI clips** for pupils but insists on checking notes and charging a clear fee.

steps.text: Require eight prepaid pupils for the four-week ear class if hall rent is low
Cancel the next ear class block if only four pupils enroll
Make checked AI practice clips for paying voice pupils
Ask the hall manager for a written live fee before next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my pupils that AGI by 2028 could write and plan music cheaply, and I would teach them to perform anyway. I would tell the hall that a live singer deserves a live fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the jingles vanish in 2028, maybe the arranging too. Stage robots come around 2031. My rent is due long before a robot joins the choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I would price the church hall and ask my father whether I can use his spare room for one evening class if the hall costs too much. If 2028 AGI kills my jingle income, I would run the class only with eight prepaid pupils and cut paid studio time first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. I can move fast, but I cannot invent a month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or cost goes first if the jingles vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio hour costs 60 each month. I would record practice clips in my bedroom if those jingle fees go, even if the sound needs more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What help could your father actually give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would lend me a room, not cash; he is keeping the repair shop open himself. I would rather teach there than ask him to cover my rent.

say: I would tell pupils that **live performance** still needs training even with cheap scores.
I would demand a **live fee** from the choir hall.
think: My **jingle income** could end in 2028, before stage robots arrive around 2031.
My father could offer a **room**, but he cannot replace my lost pay.
do: Price the **church hall** tomorrow and ask about my father’s spare room.
Run a **prepaid ear class** only with eight pupils if AGI kills jingle income.
Cancel the **60 studio hour** if 2028 AGI removes jingle fees.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because quick action cannot create a month of savings.
S2.quote: My rent is due long before a robot joins the choir.
fieldNote: She understands the **2028 income loss** can arrive before the 2031 robot stage risk.
Her family fallback is a **spare room**, explicitly not a cash cushion.

steps.text: Run a prepaid ear class with eight pupils if AGI kills jingles
Cancel the 60 studio hour if jingle fees go
Ask her father for his spare room if church hall rent is high

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that five years gives us time to train more singers and keep audiences coming. I would ask the hall for a three-year agreement, because I would rather earn security than wait for a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 would probably erase my jingle work, but I could build two paid classes by then. Robots around 2034 might imitate a choir, although I do not know whether families would buy a ticket for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with one ear class this winter if the room and eight pupils are there. If the first two blocks fill, I would add a second class next year and save half its profit; in the first year after 2031 I would keep teaching before making any stage decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be anxious until classes prove themselves. Five years lets me test whether eight people will pay for a class, not assume they will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a hall agreement actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written hall agreement would tell me how many Wednesdays I can count on. If the hall will only promise a term, I will keep building classes rather than plan rent around three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let AI take over those classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to draft practice plans, but I still listen to each pupil. I would not sell an automatic lesson as my own attention.

say: I would ask the hall for a **three-year agreement** for choir nights.
I would tell families that **AI plans** do not replace listening to a pupil.
think: Two paid **ear classes** might replace jingle money before AGI arrives in 2031.
I cannot assume a **2034 robot choir** will draw or repel an audience.
do: Start one **ear class** this winter if eight pupils and a cheap room are available.
Add a **second class** next year only if the first two blocks fill.
feel: I feel **anxious** until the classes prove they can pay.
S3.quote: Five years lets me test whether eight people will pay for a class, not assume they will.
fieldNote: Her five-year plan has **clear enrollment gates** before expanding the class or saving any profits.
Her regular **AI use** still leaves each pupil’s listening work with her.

steps.text: Start an ear class if eight pupils and a cheap room are available
Save half of second-class profit if the first two blocks fill
Keep choir teaching through the first year after 2031 AGI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my pupils that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to become better listeners and performers. I would ask younger singers to apprentice with the choir rather than wait for a perfect recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could have a dependable teaching business, though no one owes me a full class. Robots around 2039 might perform, but I suspect families will still pay to learn in a room with others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next term, I would set aside one paid class place each term for a trainee if the class covers its rent. I would build a three-month cushion from the other places over the decade, then after 2036 compare choir pay with class income before choosing which to lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about this winter’s bills, even with a longer runway. A ten-year plan does not fill next Thursday’s empty lesson slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the class can fund savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save only from a class that fills; empty chairs are not savings. I would keep a simple monthly sheet of actual fees after room rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprentice actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice should carry music stands, sing beside us and get a small fee when the hall can pay it. That is how my father taught me to value useful work.

say: I would ask younger singers to **apprentice** with the choir.
I would tell pupils a decade is time to become **better listeners**.
think: A dependable **teaching business** may exist by 2036, but each class must fill.
I expect some families to value **shared lessons** even near 2039 robots.
do: Offer one **trainee place** starting next term if class fees cover room rent.
Build a **three-month cushion** from filled class income over the decade.
feel: I feel **anxious** about present bills, despite the longer runway.
S4.quote: A ten-year plan does not fill next Thursday’s empty lesson slot.
fieldNote: She ties **apprenticeship** to a class that first pays its own room costs.
Her **current thin cushion** keeps the long scenario anxious despite an ambitious plan.

steps.text: Offer a trainee place next term if class fees cover room rent
Build a three-month cushion from filled class income
Compare choir pay and class income after 2036 AGI arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because jingle money could disappear before my classes are ready. Cheap room hire, eight prepaid pupils and a firm choir fee would help me earn through it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gives a young singer the first paid place. A choir that forgets apprentices has no human sound to defend later.

headlineQuote: A choir that forgets apprentices has no human sound to defend later.
portrait: At **27**, Hana conducts a choir, teaches voice and makes jingles despite low pay and less than a month saved.
She uses **AI daily** for practical tasks, checking messages and practice clips before they reach pupils.
Her **traditional outlook** favours earned income, apprenticeships and a room her father could lend over cash help.
She tests **prepaid classes** against room cost and enrollment before expanding or saving any profit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Hana’s jingle pay before a new class has paying pupils.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap room hire**, eight prepaid pupils and a firm choir fee would let Hana earn through the change.
